status_summary: The 2025 reconciliation law (Public Law 119-21, signed 2025-07-04) includes Sec. 20004 on munitions and defense supply chain resiliency, about $25.4 billion per CRS, plus about $16.0 billion in Sec. 20005 for scaling low-cost weapons into production. The FY2026 NDAA (Public Law 119-60, signed 2025-12-18) lists Sec. 804 on multiyear procurement authority for certain munitions, Sec. 832 on supply chain resilience and Secs. 361, 362 and 364 on munitions requirements reporting. In 2026 the Department of War signed a seven-year framework with Lockheed Martin to raise PAC-3 MSE capacity from about 600 to about 2,000 a year (announced 2026-01-06), further PAC-3, THAAD and SM-3 component frameworks in July and August, further PAC-3 and THAAD frameworks with General Dynamics and Lockheed Martin (2026-08-31), and a $22.9 billion Tomahawk contract (2026-08-17), while the Deputy Secretary asked industry on 2026-08-05 for acceleration plans on 16 programs. The Department of War Inspector General (evaluation DOWIG-2026-095, 2026-07-09) found Army 155mm output at about 36,000 rounds a month in March 2026, up from 14,000, against a 100,000 goal for October 2025 that was missed, with 140,000 a month projected by December 2027; the report says the capacity goal was based on Ukraine's consumption and that more than 3 million rounds were provided to Ukraine through presidential drawdowns.

timeline.event: Public Law 119-21 was enacted; its Title II includes Sec. 20004 (munitions and defense supply chain resiliency, $25.381 billion per CRS) and Sec. 20005 (scaling low-cost weapons into production, $16.049 billion).

The FY2026 NDAA (Public Law 119-60) was signed; its table of contents includes Sec. 804 (multiyear procurement authority for covered systems and certain munitions), Sec. 832 (supply chain resilience and secondary sources) and Secs. 361, 362 and 364 (munitions requirement and inventory reporting, including a report on munitions for simultaneous conflicts).

Lockheed Martin and the Department of War announced a seven-year framework agreement to raise PAC-3 MSE capacity from about 600 to about 2,000 a year, with an initial contract award expected through FY2026 appropriations.

The Department of War Inspector General issues evaluation DOWIG-2026-095: the goal of 100,000 155mm rounds a month by October 2025 was not met; output rose from 14,000 to 36,000 a month by March 2026, limited by load, assemble and pack capacity; capacity is projected at 63,000 by September 2026 and 140,000 by December 2027; the Army was about 11 months behind plan; and the Mesquite, Texas metal-parts site had produced no conforming parts after 469 million dollars of investment, with production moved to Pennsylvania under an April 2026 agreement.
timeline.source: Department of War Office of Inspector General (oversight.gov)

timeline.event: The Department of War announced two framework agreements worth over $3 billion with Northrop Grumman to add a second source of PAC-3 MSE rocket motors and quadruple THAAD structural component output.
The Deputy Secretary of War sent industry a memo asking for plans to accelerate delivery and raise production on 16 critical programs, with replies due 2026-08-26.

The Navy awarded RTX a $22.9 billion contract to accelerate Tomahawk production; the Navy press release of this date names the Acting Secretary of the Navy and the Under Secretary of War for Acquisition and Sustainment and does not state a duration or production rate.

The Department of War announced further seven-year framework agreements with General Dynamics Ordnance and Tactical Systems and Lockheed Martin aimed at tripling PAC-3 MSE and quadrupling THAAD interceptor production capacity; no dollar value was reported and funding is subject to annual appropriations.

title: Replenish stockpiles and produce key munitions at maximum rate
uncertainties: No section text of Public Law 119-60 or 119-21 was readable (the GovInfo HTML copies hold the table of contents and front matter), so the Sec. 804 content and covered munitions are unknown and the dollar figures come from CRS, which does not detail Sec. 20004 purposes. The PAC-3 framework rests on the company's release; no war.gov page was opened. The Munitions Acceleration Council is named only in the ExecutiveGov article as a collaborator, and its charter and date were not confirmed, so it is not used as an event. Military Times relays CSIS estimates of interceptor drawdowns after the 2026 Iran war; the reported drivers of current replenishment differ from the Ukraine support the Mandate names, and apart from the Inspector General's statement that the 155mm goal was sized to Ukraine consumption, no source tying 2025 or 2026 production steps to Ukraine stock replacement was found. The 155mm figures were confirmed in the Inspector General evaluation itself (DOWIG-2026-095, read on oversight.gov), which also ties the 155mm goal to Ukraine consumption. The Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative extension was not read. The 155mm rate also appears in c04-17. This record is the split-out of the munitions element that c04-05 says was not verified and c04-17 treats only for 155mm rounds. The PAC-3 framework is a company-announced framework, not a contract, with an initial award expected through FY2026 appropriations; the Tomahawk contract was read in the Navy press release of 2026-08-17 on navy.mil (a matching Department of War release on war.gov states no date or duration in the text read); the August 2026 framework events (2026-08-03 and 2026-08-31) were read through news and trade reports, not Department of War documents, and the copies of the 2026-08-03 release could not be opened on war.gov or globalsecurity.org in this review. Defense News (2026-08-31) attributes the 2026-08-31 frameworks to stockpiles depleted by the Iran conflict and by transfers to Ukraine, citing CSIS estimates of Patriot and THAAD expenditure; this is a news characterization, not a Department of War statement tying the frameworks to Ukraine replenishment, so the remaining item on Ukraine-linked replenishment is kept.
